name: SaaS products
title: SaaS analytics: activation, retention and churn signals
description: Product analytics for SaaS teams: funnels from signup to activation, retention cohorts by signup week, and a per-user event timeline. Cookieless and EU-hosted.
tagline: Signup to activation to paid, with a timeline for every account. Hosted in the EU.
intro: Privytics is product analytics for SaaS teams that need to see what happens after the signup form. You track anonymous events with the web SDK, call identify() with your own user id once someone logs in, and from then on funnels, retention cohorts and the per-user timeline all resolve to real accounts. Event data is stored in Germany, and the anonymous layer sets no cookies.

why.title: Your user id is the join key, not a device
why.body: A SaaS user signs up on a laptop, gets the invite email on a phone and comes back three weeks later in a different browser. identify() with the id from your own users table stitches those sessions into one profile, so activation and retention are measured per account instead of per device. This is the identified layer: it goes beyond the cookieless default, it is opt-in, and you need your own lawful basis for it.

why.title: Onboarding funnels over events you named yourself
why.body: Activation is specific to your product: created a workspace, invited a teammate, connected a source, shipped the first thing that matters. You define those steps as tracked events and build the funnel over them, so the drop-off you see is between your real steps rather than between generic pageviews.

why.title: Retention by signup week, not by calendar month
why.body: Cohorts group users by when they first appeared, so you can compare the week you changed onboarding against the week before it. That is the view that tells you whether an onboarding change actually held, which a monthly active user chart will hide for a quarter.

why.title: A per-user timeline you can open during a support thread
why.body: When a customer writes in, the profile view shows that account's events in order: what they did, in what sequence, and where it stopped. Support and product read the same timeline instead of reconstructing it from application logs.

steps.title: Install and initialise the web SDK
steps.body: Setting apiUrl is required. Without it the SDK sends events to OpenPanel's own hosted API instead of Privytics. If you would rather not add a dependency, the plain script tag from https://privytics.com/op1.js takes the same options.

steps.title: Identify the user after login
steps.body: Pass the id from your own users table as profileId. Everything tracked from that point is attributed to the profile, which is what makes cohorts and the per-user timeline work. This is the identified layer, so decide your lawful basis for it before you ship. Call clear() on logout so a shared machine does not attribute the next session to the previous account.

steps.title: Track the activation path as named events
steps.body: Keep the list short and stable. Name events after what the user did, in past tense, and put the variable parts in properties rather than in the event name. Five to ten well-chosen events give you a usable funnel; fifty ad hoc ones give you a cleanup project.

faq.q: How do I measure activation in a SaaS product?
faq.a: Pick the two or three actions that predict a user sticking around, track each as its own event, then build a funnel over them in order. Because you call identify() after login, the funnel counts accounts rather than browsers, so a user who signs up on a laptop and finishes setup on a phone still counts once.

faq.q: Can I see every event for one specific customer?
faq.a: Yes, once that user has been identified. The profile view lists that account's events in order, which is the view to open when a support thread says the product did nothing. Users who were never identified stay in the anonymous layer and have no per-account timeline.

faq.q: Do I need consent to use identify() with my own user ids?
faq.a: We cannot answer that for you, and you remain the data controller. What we can describe is the split: the default tracking layer writes no cookies and counts visitors with a daily-rotating salted hash of IP, user agent and project id. The moment you call identify() with your own user id, you are processing identifiable data about a known person and you need your own lawful basis for it.

faq.q: When is Privytics the wrong tool for a SaaS team?
faq.a: If your analytics already lives in your own warehouse and you want models built in dbt and explored in SQL, a warehouse-native stack fits better. If you need in-product messaging, surveys or feature-flag experimentation attached to the same events, those are separate product categories and we do not cover them. If your main question is paid acquisition attribution across ad platforms with server-side conversion APIs, use a marketing attribution tool. Privytics is for the product behaviour question: who activated, who came back, and where the drop-off is.

faq.q: What does it cost to start?
faq.a: The free tier is 10,000 events per month, one project and 12 months retention, with no credit card. Paid plans start at EUR 10 for 100k events per month and add session replay and 5 years of event history. Session replay is opt-in per project and masks all text and inputs by default.

omitted: No customer names, testimonials, event volumes or uptime figures appear anywhere on this page.
No comparison claiming Privytics is faster or more reliable than any other analytics tool.
No claim that using Privytics makes the reader GDPR compliant. The copy describes the design and states that the reader remains the data controller.

Churn prediction, churn scoring and any form of alerting on at-risk accounts were left out of the body copy despite the title mentioning churn signals. The product surfaces retention cohorts and per-user timelines, from which you read churn signals yourself. There is no churn model or alert feature to describe.

MRR, ARR, LTV and other revenue metrics were not presented as built-in. The SDK does have a revenue() helper and a __revenue property, but the amount must be an integer and no SaaS billing integration was verified, so no revenue snippet was shown.

Group and workspace analytics were omitted from the snippets. setGroup, setGroups and upsertGroup are real methods on the SDK and are the natural fit for B2B account-level rollups, but no Privytics-facing docs page for them was checked, so workspace_id is shown as a plain property instead.
increment() and decrement() on profile properties are real and would suit counters like seats_used, but they were cut to keep the taxonomy step to one idea.

Server-side tracking was omitted. A SaaS team would reasonably want billing webhooks tracked from the backend with a clientSecret, but this page is scoped to the browser SDK. Point readers at the Node or framework SDK pages for that.
scriptUrl is not shown. It is only relevant for framework components that inject a script tag for you, not for the npm web SDK. The plain script tag URL is mentioned in prose only.
Session replay setup code was not included. Replay is paid-plan and opt-in per project, and no complete Privytics-specific config example was verified.
Salt rotation is described as daily in the copy. The salt rotates at midnight UTC, but the audience page keeps the shorter phrasing and leaves the exact rotation time to the SDK and docs pages.
docsUrl was left off. No Privytics-hosted or upstream OpenPanel docs page covers this audience page as a topic.
